missing_spec_content.spec_text: Typical values may be taken as: walking ~ 1.5 m/s running ~ 3 m/s cycling ~ 6 m/s.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson lists typical speeds for walking, cycling, a motorway car, sound and light. It never gives the typical running speed (~3 m/s), which students must recall.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to recall typical values of speed for a person walking, running and cycling as well as the typical values of speed for different types of transportation systems.
missing_spec_content.why: The only transport speed given is a car on a motorway (≈ 30 m/s). No other types of transportation system are covered.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The speed of a moving object is rarely constant. When people walk, run or travel in a car their speed is constantly changing. The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on many factors including: age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not say that real speeds vary, or which factors affect walking, running and cycling speeds.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: It is not only moving objects that have varying speed. The speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives 330 m/s for sound but does not say that the speed of sound and wind speed vary.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to make measurements of distance and time and then calculate speeds of objects.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not teach how to measure distance and time to find a speed. It only calculates speed from given values.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) Students should be able to explain qualitatively, with examples, that motion in a circle involves constant speed but changing velocity.
missing_spec_content.why: Circular motion (constant speed, changing velocity) is not taught anywhere in the lesson.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time can be determined by drawing a tangent and measuring the gradient of the distance–time graph at that time.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson says a curved d-t line means changing speed. It never teaches drawing a tangent to find the speed at a given time.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to estimate the magnitude of everyday accelerations.
missing_spec_content.why: No typical everyday accelerations are given or estimated.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) measure, when appropriate, the area under a velocity–time graph by counting squares.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson only covers areas of triangles and trapeziums. It does not teach counting squares, which is needed for curved v-t graphs.

above_gcse.why: This equation is not in the specification. The spec gives only a = Δv/t and v² − u² = 2as. Presenting a full SUVAT set adds a method the student is not required to know and could confuse them.

above_gcse.text: These equations link the five motion quantities: ... You are given three values and asked to find a fourth.
above_gcse.why: The 'SUVAT' five-variable framework is A-level style. The spec only requires recalling and applying a = Δv/t and applying v² − u² = 2as.

above_gcse.text: Displacement = 500m, in a direction about 53° north of east.
above_gcse.why: Finding the 53° angle needs trigonometry (inverse tangent), which this section does not require. The student is not shown how to get the angle, so this could confuse them.

wrong_terms.text: Equation: v = d/t. Rearrangements: d = vt, t = d/v.
wrong_terms.spec_term: distance travelled = speed × time, s = v t (distance, s, in metres)
distance, s, in metres, m (in v² − u² = 2 a s)
